slides.title: Why Geometric Algebra?
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as a design problem for geometry software. The audience already knows vectors and matrices, so the useful question is not whether those tools work, but why a larger algebra can make geometric intent easier to preserve across constructions, measurements, and transformations.

slides.title: The Fragmentation Problem
slides.notes: Use the diagram as a diagnosis of ordinary geometric programming. Each classical representation is reasonable in isolation, but the application pays a translation tax whenever a line, circle, plane, rotation, or inversion must interact with another object whose data lives in a different formalism.

slides.title: The Core Change
slides.notes: The key point is that geometric algebra does not merely store coordinates in a wider vector. It assigns computational meaning to grades: vectors model directed one dimensional quantities, bivectors model oriented areas, trivectors model oriented volumes, and mixed multivectors let the program keep several geometric roles in one algebraic environment.

slides.title: Outer Product As Construction
slides.notes: Treat the parallelogram and circle together. The outer product records independence and orientation, so it can build an area element from two vectors and, in richer models, a round object from point handles. The numerical notebook uses coordinate stand-ins, but the invariant habit is already visible.

slides.title: Rotations Act On Whole Objects
slides.notes: Stress that rotor language is about object level action. A matrix can rotate sampled points, but the geometric algebra pattern packages the motion as an algebra element that sandwiches the object. The same conceptual operation then applies to vectors, planes, circles, and later conformal primitives.

slides.title: Objects Can Be Operators
slides.notes: The mirror visual should make a philosophical point concrete: a plane is not only a set of points satisfying an equation. In geometric algebra, the element representing the mirror can also drive the reflection operation, so representation and action become two uses of the same geometric object.

slides.title: Sphere Inversion As A Unifying Test
slides.notes: The inversion picture prepares students for the conformal model without formal machinery. Planes and spheres will later live in one family, and their actions become versor operations. For now, the reciprocal distance identity gives a simple invariant that distinguishes inversion from rigid reflection.

slides.title: Interpolation Comes From Operators
slides.notes: Interpolation is where the operator viewpoint starts to feel practical. Instead of inventing a separate blending rule for every motion type, the algebraic route asks for the logarithm of the motion element and applies fractional powers. The familiar rotation case becomes one member of a wider pattern.

slides.title: Programming Payoff
slides.notes: Use this as a software design slide, not as a sales pitch. The payoff is that high level code can ask for constructions, actions, and checks in geometric terms, while optimized product implementations handle the algebraic details. The notebook sanity checks demonstrate the testing habit that keeps abstraction honest.

slides.title: Route Through The Book
slides.notes: Close by treating the chapter as a promise with a payment plan. The first lecture motivates the shared language, then the next chapters add outer products, metric products, complements, meets, joins, the geometric product, rotors, and models of Euclidean geometry until the opening examples become native algebraic operations.
